issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of appellant Nos. 2 and 3 for the offence punishable under Section 302 IPC should be upheld.

facts: The only evidence linking appellants Nos. 2 and 3 to the murder was the confession of the co-accused, appellant No. 1, made to the police.
The prosecution did not produce any other substantive evidence to show that appellants Nos. 2 and 3 were involved in causing the murder.
law: A person cannot be convicted for an offence solely on the basis of a confession made by a co-accused to the police.
A conviction for murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) requires substantive evidence showing the accused's involvement in the act.

When a charge is framed 'simpliciter' under Section 302, without invoking sections for shared liability like Section 34 (common intention) or Section 120-B (criminal conspiracy), the prosecution must prove the individual's role in the murder.
application: The Court found that there was no substantive evidence to prove the involvement of appellants Nos. 2 and 3 in the murder of the two victims.
The Court determined that it was not permissible to convict them based only on the confession of their co-accused, appellant No. 1.

The Court also noted a procedural flaw: the charge was framed simply under Section 302, not under Section 302 read with Section 34 or 120-B, which would have been necessary to establish shared guilt without proving their individual acts of murder. The prosecution failed to produce evidence to support even this simple charge against them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the conviction of appellants Nos. 2 and 3 for murder under Section 302 IPC because there was a complete lack of substantive evidence showing their involvement in the crime. The conviction could not be sustained solely on the confession of a co-accused, and the charge was not framed in a way that would support a conviction based on shared liability.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of appellant Nos. 2 and 3 for the offence punishable under Section 201 IPC should be upheld.

facts: Appellants Nos. 2 and 3 lived in the same house as the deceased, who were their close relatives (wife/step-mother and son/step-brother).
The deceased suddenly went missing for over two months.
Appellants Nos. 2 and 3 made no effort to trace the deceased nor did they report their disappearance to the police.
The dead bodies of the deceased were eventually found in a septic tank in the backyard of the appellants' house.
The appellants offered no explanation for their failure to report the disappearance of their family members.
law: Section 201 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) pertains to the offence of causing the disappearance of evidence of an offence or giving false information to screen the offender from legal punishment.
application: The Court found the appellants' failure to report the disappearance of their close family members for two months to be unnatural conduct.

From the proved circumstances and the appellants' "abject failure to offer any explanation," the Court deduced that they had knowledge that the deceased had been murdered and their bodies were dumped in the septic tank.
The Court concluded that by not disclosing this fact, the appellants' intention was to screen appellant No. 1, the main offender, from legal punishment.
Even though there was a lack of legal evidence to convict them for the murder itself (under Section 302 IPC), their conduct established their guilt for the separate offence under Section 201 IPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of appellants Nos. 2 and 3 under Section 201 IPC because the established circumstances and their failure to explain their unnatural conduct proved they had knowledge of the murders and intentionally concealed that information to protect the main offender from legal punishment.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: It is not permissible to proceed against appellant nos.2 and 3 solely on the basis of the confession of appellant No.1 made before the police. Even if a relevant part of the confession is admissible (under Section 27 of the Evidence Act), it cannot serve as the substantive evidence required to convict a co-accused in the absence of other corroborating evidence.
legal_tests_applied: A conviction cannot be sustained solely on the basis of a confession made by a co-accused to the police, as it is not considered substantive evidence against the other accused.

In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must establish two conditions: (1) the circumstances from which an inference of guilt is sought to be drawn must be cogently and firmly established; and (2) those circumstances should be of a definite tendency unerringly pointing towards the guilt of the accused.

policy_considerations: The rule against convicting an accused solely on the basis of a co-accused's confession to the police serves as a fundamental safeguard against wrongful convictions, recognizing that such confessions may be unreliable and do not constitute substantive evidence against anyone other than the confessor.
